summary: Suggests a pair of TCP options for using alternate data checksum algorithms in the TCP header, and corrects errors introduced in editing RFC 1145. It is experimental and not for production. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6247.

eli5.summary: Packets have a check number to catch mistakes. This is a fixed copy of the note about using a different way to compute it.

questions: what are tcp alternate checksum options
subtitle: Options to negotiate different error-detection algorithms during TCP connection setup.

tldr.problem: The standard TCP checksum is limited for some error-detection needs; some systems want to use stronger or more specialized checksum algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: Two new TCP options allow endpoints to request and negotiate an alternate checksum algorithm (such as Fletcher's) at connection establishment, with a separate option to carry checksums longer than 16 bits.
tldr.outcome: This was marked Historic and superseded by RFC 6247. The mechanism proved experimental and never saw widespread adoption.

today: RFC 1146 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6247 in 2011. The alternate checksum negotiation mechanism never achieved significant deployment.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The standard TCP checksum, defined in RFC 793, detects some errors but has limits. RFC 1146 proposes two TCP options to let endpoints negotiate the use of a different checksum algorithm at connection time. The options also handle checksums longer than the standard 16 bits.

The mechanism is experimental and the authors do not recommend it for production use. The RFC corrects errors that were introduced in RFC 1145.
sections.eli5: When two computers connect, they can exchange a message saying 'let's use a different check number method' instead of the standard one.

sections.title: The Checksum Options
sections.content:
RFC 1146 defines two TCP options negotiated during the three-way handshake.

The TCP Alternate Checksum Request Option (Kind=14, Length=3) carries a number identifying the checksum algorithm. It may be sent in a SYN segment by either endpoint. If both SYN segments specify the same algorithm, that algorithm is used for the rest of the connection. If they disagree, or if one does not send the option, the connection falls back to the standard TCP checksum. SYN and RST segments always use the standard checksum, ensuring compatibility even if negotiation fails.

The TCP Alternate Checksum Data Option (Kind=15) carries additional checksum bytes when the chosen algorithm produces more than 16 bits. The checksum field in the TCP header may be split between the standard location and this option, or the entire checksum may be placed in the option.
sections.eli5: The request option asks 'can we use method X?' The data option holds extra check bytes when the method produces big numbers. Both sides must agree on the method, or they give up and use the standard way.

sections.title: Supported Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 1146 defines three checksum algorithms by number: 0 for the standard TCP checksum, 1 for the 8-bit Fletcher algorithm, and 2 for the 16-bit Fletcher algorithm.

The 8-bit Fletcher algorithm produces a 16-bit checksum by maintaining two 8-bit accumulators over the data, one for simple sum and one for a weighted sum. This detects transposed bytes and words. The 16-bit Fletcher algorithm uses 16-bit accumulators and produces a 32-bit result, stored partly in the header checksum field and partly in the data option.

The appendices give the exact algorithms and note faster implementations exist; RFC 1146 permits any computation that produces the same numeric result as the loop definition.
sections.eli5: Method 1 and method 2 are both called Fletcher checksums, a way to calculate check numbers by keeping running totals. Method 1 gives a small number; method 2 gives a bigger one.
